blocks.text: I downloaded 400 million+ Polymarket trades totaling 36 GB and gave AI just one task: find statistical relationships, pricing inefficiencies and recurring structural advantages

After 2.5 weeks of analysis and simulations of different statistics, I found 2 Polymarket inefficiencies that could potentially generate tens of thousands of dollars per month

I also found traders who discovered these inefficiencies before me and quietly built trading strategies around them that have already made them more than $140k

Next I'll show exactly how these 2 inefficiencies work and how they are already being used in practice
Let's get straight to it
Here is the dataset I used for the analysis:
https://x.com/beckerrjon/status/2021280975318040917

This is Jon Becker's repository with the largest publicly available dataset collected over 5 years: more than 400 million trades from Polymarket and Kalshi (For this article I only used the Polymarket part)

It contains full metadata for each market, detailed trade data and resolution results
1 Inefficiency: what happens more often after touching 90% / 10%
The first few hours of analysis gave me nothing interesting at all
I was already starting to think there was nothing interesting in this data
But around the fifth hour, I spontaneously had the idea to check where the market statistically goes after touching 90% or 10% odds

I analyzed 4,317 markets that reached those odds and looked at which path the price more often takes next

And this is where the results became truly interesting:

At first glance, it may seem like there is nothing unusual here

But if you look more closely, an important property of the market becomes visible: even after reaching an extreme probability, the price still quite often makes a strong pullback toward the middle or even goes even deeper in the opposite direction

This is exactly where a powerful inefficiency appears:

90c/10c levels do not mean a stable fixation of probability. Historically, the market often shows mean reversion back to 50c and in some cases continues moving to 20c/80c

Here is a simple explanation with an example:

Let's say there is a $100 bankroll and 100 markets where the price is as close as possible to 90c / 10c

If you place $1 limit orders on each market, the picture looks like this:
6% = 6 markets make a move equivalent to about 800% profit
13% = 13 markets make a move equivalent to about 500% profit
the remaining 80% end in a loss
So in a rough model, it looks like this:
Examples of traders most likely using this inefficiency:
mocamoca (made $45,847 in 2 months)
His strategy: he places buy limit orders at 3-15c and after building positions he places sell limit orders in the 87-93c zone
https://polymarket.com/@mocamoca?via=paon-guioner-yazy
planktonXD (made $99,056 in 3 months)

The logic is similar, but even more aggressive: building positions at 1-2c and trying to close closer to 90-100c

https://polymarket.com/@planktonXD?via=paon-guioner-yazy
They both opened hundreds of positions without even looking at the market title because they know that statistically they will win
2 Inefficiency: Price magnets where probabilities statistically flow

After finding the first inefficiency I decided to dig deeper

And after a few more hours of analysis, AI found another detail that at first looks trivial, but is actually very important:
Prices in prediction markets are distributed unevenly and historically probabilities cluster around 0-5c, 25c, 50c, 75c and 95-100c
I noticed this after AI output the distribution of current probabilities across a random sample of 800 Polymarket markets

Visually, you can clearly see that the market does not cluster evenly, but around several specific levels

But the most interesting part was not the existence of these levels themselves but the fact that after reaching the 75c / 25c zone, the market statistically more often returns to the middle, meaning 50c
If we translate this into a rough model for 100 markets at $1 each, the picture looks like this:
In 54 markets, the limit order at 50c gets filled, which gives about x2 and $108 in total
In 46 markets, the position loses all its value

So in this simplified simulation based purely on statistics, the result looks like about +8% on the initial capital

At the moment, I am personally testing this inefficiency on real markets
Later I will share my results in a separate post
So if you want to see not only historical statistics but also a live result, you can follow now
Useful addition: how long this movement usually takes
When I found the previous 2 inefficiencies, the next question immediately came to my mind:
How long do you need to hold the position for this statistic to turn into real profit?
To answer it, I asked AI to separately analyze the time it takes for the market to pass key routes:
The sample included about 1,100 markets, after which I got the holding time distribution and average values for each route
To estimate what such a strategy could look like on a yearly basis, I used a simple APY formula:
APY = \frac{Hours.per.year}{Hours.per.period} \times Return.per.period
where:
Hours per year = total number of hours in a year = 8760
Hours per cycle = the average time it takes for the market to complete the required route
Return per cycle = the average return of one such trade based on my model

In theory, this gives an incredible 1372% and 2190% profit per year 👀
In conclusion, I want to say the main thing:

These are not random observations and not just a couple of pretty screenshots

These are measurement results from the largest publicly available prediction markets dataset that I managed to run through my own analysis and AI pipeline
The data described above can potentially bring in thousands of dollars if you know how to use it and those who found it before me have already made a fortune

But keep in mind that all of these inefficiencies still require careful verification

Right now I am testing both ideas on real markets

In the coming week I plan to test both of these inefficiencies and when I have a concrete result, I will separately show what actually works in practice and what only looks beautiful in historical data
So if you are interested in real edge in prediction markets, you can follow now so you don't miss the continuation
And always:
do your own research

result.text:
The reversion signal is real but the edge is smaller than it looks once you model:
- fill rates (liquidity at 3-15c is almost nonexistent on most markets)
- capital idle time (kills that APY by 5-10x)
- survivorship bias (2 winners ≠ strategy validation)

The 25/50/75 clustering is the more interesting finding imo. It's structural, not behavioral — driven by market maker grid placement and resolution mechanics.
